Read keys expose the wider event context, many pollers can overload the instance, and devices that accept only single addresses cannot use CIDR ranges without expansion. The speaker presents Katos, a FastAPI service with Memcached as a caching layer, that sits between MISP and security tools and serves only indicators as feeds. Feeds can be filtered by tags, IDS flags, publish state and warning lists, with deduplication and regex checks on fields such as IP. A repeated one-year query dropped from about 2.3 seconds to under a second, and cache entries expire automatically.

Access is limited through IP allowlists and per-instance tokens tied to the MISP security model. Future work includes better documentation, data minimisation and more output formats. The release is aimed at community feedback, and the takeaway is that a caching proxy lets detection tools use MISP data without exposing the whole instance.

talks.title: Why Does The CTI Industry Struggle With Communicating Uncertainties?
talks.teaser: Explains how CTI reports express uncertainty and compares common likelihood and confidence wording across vendors.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a CTI analyst with a government intelligence background, starts with where uncertainty comes from in threat intelligence work. Analysts rarely have complete information, human behaviour is hard to model, and predictive judgments are themselves a source of doubt. Analysts often soften their wording with phrases such as "probably" or "we believe", and those phrases are easily read in different ways.

The talk separates two concepts that are often mixed up. Words of estimative probability describe how likely a judgment is, while levels of confidence describe how well the judgment is supported by sources, rated low, moderate or high. The speaker showed example sentences that combine the two, and noted that a small comparison of four vendor reports found inconsistent use, with some using only one expression and one mixing both without a clear reason. A five-level likelihood scale was presented, along with rough evidence criteria, such as strong supporting evidence and a history of similar events, for choosing terms like "highly likely".

In the Q&A, the speaker explained that likelihood and confidence describe different things, so a well-sourced claim can still be unlikely. Numeric percentages were discouraged because the estimates are qualitative. The closing advice is to keep the approach simple, apply it consistently, be transparent about the terms used, and explain why a given level was chosen.

talks.title: Kunai: Your New Threat Hunting Tool For Linux
talks.teaser: Introduces Kunai, an eBPF-based Linux monitoring tool for threat hunting, and explains how it was built.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an independent incident response consultant, introduces Kunai, a Linux monitoring tool for threat hunting intended to fill the gap left by Sysmon on Windows. His objections to the existing Linux port covered its XML configuration, a C++ codebase that is hard to collaborate on, a Windows-style event set that fits Linux poorly, and a repository that had gone quiet. His goals were to keep the useful ideas, balance raw and over-processed events, and provide solid documentation.

Kunai relies on eBPF rather than a kernel module. eBPF programs pass a verifier, run in a sandboxed virtual machine inside the kernel, attach to many kernel points, and share data with user space through maps. Rust was chosen so one language covers both kernel and user-space code, using the Aya library. The speaker also describes the learning curve, a mid-project library switch, and upstream contributions. Features include process tracking by unique IDs, events for executed and memory-mapped files, chronological JSON output, and host-side correlation, such as attaching a hostname to a connection using an earlier DNS event. Container activity is harder because files inside containers are not visible from the host.

Using CO-RE, a single binary runs on LTS kernels from 5.4 to 6.1, and the project's CI tests each kernel. Future development depends on funding and includes new probes. In questions, the speaker suggested Android could work but doubted Apple's kernel supports the needed eBPF features.

talks.title: FOSStering An ISAC: Enabling A Community With Open-Source Tools
talks.teaser: Shows how an information sharing community can be set up and run using open-source tools.

talks.title: CTI Is Dead, Long Live CTI!
talks.teaser: Explores how threat intelligence teams can time and tailor their support for incident response teams during active cases.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a debate over whether cyber threat intelligence still has a place alongside incident response teams. The speaker, a senior threat analyst at a Swiss managed security provider, frames the purpose of intelligence as preparing for attacks that have not yet happened. Incident response teams see successful intrusions and high-severity alerts first hand, which makes their findings valuable to intelligence work, while intelligence teams need actionable findings shared quickly.

The middle of the talk uses firefighting as an analogy. Responders move through a fast cycle of assessing the situation, containing damage and regaining control of the network, and they are most focused and least responsive during that sprint. The speaker maps the work of an intelligence team against this rhythm, describing it as steadier and broader, covering threat landscape tracking and sector trends. Useful windows for contribution appear at the start of a case, during hunting and scoping, and in the case summary afterwards. Suggested contributions include concise written landscape notes early on, indicators or detection ideas during the hunt, and a second opinion once responders have time to reflect.

The closing section covers points of friction. Analysts make errors that responders cannot afford under pressure, and repeated requests for customer approvals add load. Open communication channels, succinct written input tailored to the case, and discussing hypotheses once pressure drops are offered as practical approaches. The speaker concludes that intelligence teams add lasting value to incident response teams when they pay attention to pacing and context.

talks.title: Cloaking Malicious Web Content Delivery
talks.teaser: Shows how browser fingerprinting lets attackers serve malicious content only to chosen targets while showing benign pages to analysts.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces browser fingerprinting by comparing it to the guessing game Guess Who: a set of attributes collected from a browser can narrow it down to a single unique identity. One example given is canvas fingerprinting, where an image rendered in the browser varies with its hardware and settings, and the resulting data is sent back to a server.

The speaker then moves to cloaking, where a server changes what it delivers based on a visitor's fingerprint. An attacker could target a specific browser version or even a particular person, showing harmless content to everyone else and the malicious payload only to the chosen device. A decoy page can also waste an analyst's time, because the investigator may look at the benign content, decide the lead is bad, and never receive the real payload.

The main takeaway is that analysts should not assume every visit returns the same content, and that using different browser profiles may help reveal what is actually served. The speaker also points out that threat intelligence has little precise terminology for this behaviour, since existing tags describe only basic checks such as a browser version. The call is to share examples and, if the pattern recurs, to work toward a shared taxonomy.

talks.title: The Composition Analysis Of Binary Java, ELF, Go, And JavaScript Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how to match compiled Java, ELF, Go and JavaScript binaries back to the source code they came from.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a practical problem: when you are handed binaries, you often need to know which parts come from your own source checkout and which parts came from elsewhere, such as open source packages, commercial prebuilt vendor components, or code that someone may have slipped in. Unidentified origins can hide bugs or unwanted functionality. The speaker gives the example of vendor-relocated copies of Log4j, which are bundled inside other published jars under different package paths.

The middle of the talk covers techniques for each format. For Java, class file paths usually mirror the original source file names, so mapping file names by path is a first step, followed by comparing symbols, function names and strings. Decompiling and comparing against a recompiled version of the source is another option, though decompiled names often differ from the source. JavaScript is treated as a binary in practice, since it is shipped minified or transpiled. Source maps, where present, can be used to match strings and confirm origins. For ELF files, DWARF debug information records source paths, which helps map symbols precisely, and mangled C++ names can make matching even more efficient. Go binaries keep a line table even in non-debug builds, so extracted symbols and lines can be matched back to source files efficiently.

The takeaway for practitioners is that each ecosystem leaves metadata that can be used to trace where code came from. Combining these clues gives a way to account for the origin of components in a build and to spot code that does not belong.

talks.title: GeoOpen And MMDB-Server: An Open Source Solution For IP Address Geoloc.
talks.teaser: Presents a free, regularly updated IP geolocation database and a local server for querying it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common pain point in threat intelligence work: IP geolocation data. Commercial sources often require registration and payment, and historical records are usually locked behind paid tiers. Many analysts instead turn to public lookup websites, which means they hand over the addresses they are investigating. Forensic work makes this worse, because an address's location can change over months or a year, so older geolocation data is often needed.

The speaker introduces GeoOpen, a free geolocation database distributed in the MaxMind DB format. Because that format is open, the files can be read by existing tools, and users can also build their own files from their own sources. The project refreshes its data daily and publishes historical snapshots of both location and network ownership data for download. Alongside the data, the MMDB-Server project offers an open source server that loads these files and answers lookups through an API. It has integrations for MISP and other tools, and it returns location and historical records for an address. Because it runs locally, queries stay off the internet and responses are fast. A public lookup service runs the same code for people who prefer not to host anything. The lookups cover both IPv4 and IPv6.

The practical takeaway is that teams can replace ad hoc lookup websites and paid historical feeds with a local, open data source that is easy to version and swap into MaxMind-compatible workflows.

talks.title: Case Management
talks.teaser: Shows a lightweight open-source case management tool for tracking tasks, notes, reports and deadlines across organizations.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents a case management application built to be flexible across different kinds of investigations and to stay light, so the key information can be seen quickly. The demo starts with a list of cases showing each one's title, description, last modification and status, with options to complete, edit or delete. Opening a case reveals its tasks, which can be assigned to users, given a status, and expanded with attached files and notes.

Notes are written in markdown and can include Mermaid diagrams, and a report can be exported as PDF. Assigning a user to a task triggers a notification and places the task in that user's view. The tool supports several organizations, so teams can avoid duplicating work or creating entries that already exist. A calendar displays case and task creation dates and deadlines. Cases with their tasks can be imported from a structured file, and templates let a team reuse a baseline methodology, such as one for forensic investigations.

The speaker says the project is open source, hosted on GitHub, and under active development, and invites feedback through issues and pull requests. For practitioners, the main takeaway is a simple option for organizing investigation work, tracking responsibilities and producing reports, with room to shape it through contributions.

talks.title: Token Smart Contract Analyzer
talks.teaser: Shows how simulating ERC-20 tokens on a controlled node can reveal backdoors and sell restrictions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces an in-progress analyzer for spotting fraudulent ERC-20 tokens on Ethereum and Binance Smart Chain. The presenter starts with the threat model: a token's behavior is governed by its smart contract, and whoever controls the deployment can embed logic that drains liquidity, traps holders, or blocks sales. Typical patterns include backdoors that let certain parties pull funds and restrictions where a token can be bought but not sold.

The approach is to take a snapshot of the current chain state, deploy the contract onto a node the team controls, and run it to see what is actually possible. This reveals whether selling works, which fees apply, and how supply and burn figures look.

In the live demo, the presenter pasted a token address into the tool, which deployed the contract and reported supply data, buy and sell fees, and a risk section. That section flagged a remaining owner address and whitelist or blacklist controls that determine who may trade. Findings feed a set of risk tables that produce a score, and the demo token scored around 30 out of 100. The presenter closed by planning to add machine learning to automate the process and extend coverage. The practical takeaway is that simulating a token on a controlled node can expose trading restrictions that reading the code alone may not make obvious.

talks.title: SBOMs: Are They A Threat Or A Menace?
talks.teaser: Explains software bills of materials, the standards behind them, and why vulnerability data and tooling still fall short.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the growing number of third-party packages in modern software, where a commercial application can pull in ten thousand components and spreadsheets stop being useful for tracking them. It introduces the software bill of materials, borrowed from manufacturing, as a machine-readable inventory of the components used to build a product, covering where each one comes from, its name, its version and optionally its license. The speaker walks through ways to produce one: parsing manifests and lock files, reading package databases, matching files by checksum or approximate similarity, instrumenting builds, and comparing binaries against source.

The middle section covers the two main formats, SPDX and CycloneDX, which the speaker treats as interchangeable containers rather than something to fight over. It also explains the package URL identifier, which maps components to vulnerability databases more cleanly than the older CPE scheme. The speaker argues that keeping component lists secret does not provide real security, and that exchange documents such as VEX are needed to state which known issues actually apply to a given product. Regulatory pressure is covered too, including a recent US executive order and upcoming European rules that could require disclosure, even for some open-source projects.

The closing part identifies the gaps. Few tools can ingest SBOMs on the receiving end, commercial vulnerability feeds often contain invented versions and packages, and the current curation process does not scale. The takeaway is that SBOMs are moving toward becoming a mandate, that the community needs better and more reliable vulnerability data, and that open-source maintainers face a compliance burden they did not sign up for and have no funding to cover.

talks.title: Detecting VPNs/Proxies By Analyzing Their Attack Patterns Over Time
talks.teaser: Shows how crowdsourced intrusion data can reveal VPN and proxy addresses through their shifting attack patterns over time.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how crowdsourced intrusion data from an open-source intrusion prevention system can be used to spot VPN and proxy addresses. The data only records abusive activity, so anonymized services with mostly legitimate users show up as gaps and irregular bursts rather than steady traffic.

The analysis has two parts. A static view compares which attack scenarios are more common from proxy addresses than from other addresses. Brute-force attempts tend to come from compromised hosts, while spam comments often arrive through anonymized traffic, which suggests attackers rely on anonymization when interrupted attacks still succeed. The dynamic view groups each address's daily mix of attack types into clusters, so small day-to-day variation counts as the same pattern while major shifts count as changes. Frequent changes in cluster membership, along with missing days and erratic activity, point toward a proxy or VPN.

These signals feed a machine learning model trained on externally sourced labels. The model is tuned for recall, which accepts many false positives, and the speaker notes that some of these were later confirmed as unlabeled anonymizers. The pipeline runs serverless on AWS and takes about half a second per lookup. The talk closes with a public labeled dataset released as a competition, giving practitioners a way to build and test their own models.

talks.title: Sbud: Infovis In Infosec
talks.teaser: Shows how a JSON-driven SVG renderer replaces hand-drawn hex editor screenshots for file format diagrams.
talks.summary:
Analysts often document binary file structures by taking screenshots of hex editors and adding arrows and labels in drawing tools. Ange Albertini, who works on malware analysis at Google's Flare team, explains why this approach is slow, inconsistent across viewers and themes, and produces images that cannot be reused when a report, slide deck or translation needs updating. He walks through his earlier attempts at automating the diagrams, including a layout system based on constraint solving that became too hard to debug.

The current version, called Sbud, takes a JSON description of the bytes, labels and highlights, then generates SVG directly with no framework and no external dependencies, so it works offline in an isolated virtual machine. Albertini demonstrated switching themes and fonts, skipping large empty regions such as padding in disc images, and exporting to PDF or PNG at chosen dimensions. He noted that bit-level and character-based formats need special handling, that the tool cannot list installed fonts without enabling fingerprinting, and that existing parsers can already emit compatible JSON.

The main takeaway is to keep the underlying information rather than the picture. Once a structure is described, the same data can be regenerated for new layouts, localisations or house styles, and the output stays vector-based. The tool is open source under the MIT license and remains experimental, with planned additions such as source code views, timelines and packet diagrams.

talks.title: CTI Operational Procedures With Jupyter Notebooks And MISP
talks.teaser: Shows how Jupyter notebooks and PyMISP turn threat intelligence investigation steps into shareable, documented procedures.
talks.summary:
Koen Van Impe starts from a common problem in cyber threat intelligence work: operational procedures live in documents that quickly fall out of date. Analysts copy commands into a virtual environment, paste the output into a report, and the written steps drift away from what the tooling now requires. He describes consumer and producer versions of such procedures, such as checking an IP address against feeds and internal MISP instances, then enriching it with ownership and DNS lookups, or guiding a junior analyst to encode attributes into a MISP event.

The middle of the talk presents Jupyter notebooks as one place to hold code, its output and explanatory text, stored as JSON so version tracking works. He walks through starting a notebook server safely, including binding it to a reachable address, using the access token, keeping API keys out of the notebook, and running it in a managed environment rather than on the MISP server itself. Practical habits include a skeleton script, separating variables from logic, printing results at each step, and clearing outputs before saving. He also shows an integration example that wraps a third-party API.

He closes with limits and ideas. Notebooks are effectively single-user unless paired with JupyterHub, resource use needs watching, and future work could link notebooks with MISP workflows. The audience questions covered whether to store notebooks with or without results, and whether this kind of tooling belongs inside the MISP interface.

talks.title: The Holy Grail For STIX And MISP Format
talks.teaser: Covers how MISP-STIX conversion grew into a standalone library, and the mapping gaps still open.
talks.summary:
Christian Studer, a MISP core developer and OASIS CTI participant, looks at how the project's STIX integration has developed and where it still falls short. He starts with the original export from MISP to STIX 1.1 and 2.0, and the limits that came with it: exports could only work on whole events, and feeds had to be imported into a MISP instance before any conversion could happen.

The middle of the talk covers the response: a standalone Python library in its own repository, now with STIX 2.1 support, attribute-level conversion, command-line use, and generated mapping documentation. The speaker describes vendor STIX bundles that fail strict UUID validation, which led the team to a more permissive loader that keeps references to the original identifiers. Custom objects fill gaps where STIX lacks required fields, while indicator patterns, course-of-action semantics and the choice between objects, attributes and galaxy clusters remain open questions.

The closing section lays out the roadmap: importing STIX 2.1 into MISP, TAXII support, exporting individual objects, and closer work with standards partners. A short live demo shows a STIX file uploaded and turned into a MISP event. The takeaway for practitioners is that conversion between the two formats is never fully lossless, so sample files and clear issue reports matter.

talks.title: WHIDS Update
talks.teaser: Walks through the latest updates to an EDR agent and manager, covering ETW support, per-rule actions and centralized configuration.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an update on a self-built endpoint detection and response project with two parts: an agent on each endpoint that reads Sysmon logs and applies custom detection rules in real time, and a manager that exposes APIs for administrators and for the agents. The speaker first recaps the core capabilities. When an alert fires, the agent can capture process memory, registry changes or a structured JSON report within seconds, and it can kill or blacklist processes. The manager handles endpoints, logs, stored artifacts and aggregated detection reports that help rank machines for triage. Events can also be streamed over a websocket to plugins, with MISP integrations as examples.

The main part covers what changed over the past year. Response actions can now be set per rule instead of only by alert criticality. Sysmon and OSQuery deployment and configuration, previously done by hand on each machine, can be pushed from the manager, and the agent configuration is centralized the same way. Indicator handling was decoupled from MISP through a generic API, so any data source can feed it. On Windows, the agent moved from hooking the older event log API to consuming ETW, which the speaker presents as faster, more flexible and less exposed to a known evasion. API documentation is now generated from tests through a git hook, and a CI/CD pipeline was built.

The talk closes with next steps: finishing a long-delayed release, publishing real attack and malware case studies, and eventually porting to Linux and macOS, where the speaker says no framework matches Sysmon's telemetry. In the Q&A, API hooking was rejected as intrusive and easy for malware to bypass in user mode. The speaker invited feedback, feature requests, code contributions and sponsorship.

talks.title: Community Orchestration Via Cerebrate
talks.teaser: Explains how Cerebrate centralizes contacts, sharing groups and keys across MISP instances for a threat-sharing community.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Cerebrate, an open-source tool built within an EU-funded project to help information-sharing communities manage their members and interconnections. The speaker describes the problems that grow with large, diverse communities: keeping track of who the partners are, finding the right CERT for a compromised system, resolving clashing identifiers when organisations join several communities, and setting up links between MISP instances by hand, which is slow and error-prone.

The middle of the talk walks through how the tool works. Cerebrate nodes exchange metadata about organisations, individuals, PGP keys and sharing groups. Two nodes can agree to interconnect through a request and confirmation handshake, after which the tool instructs the MISP instances on each side to set up the sync link, and the data then flows through the native APIs. Communities can define custom metadata libraries, connectors can manage other tools, and user management, auditing and an API are included. An opt-in public listing of organisations and a planned distinction between trusted upstream sources and ordinary feeds were also presented.

For practitioners, the main takeaway is that contact, key and sharing-group coordination can be centralised instead of run through email exchanges, though trust between members still depends on building relationships over time. The speaker closes with the roadmap, which covers signing and encrypting sharing groups, further integrations such as ticketing and messaging, and a shared codebase that will move MISP onto the same stack.

talks.title: DocIntel: A Context-Centric Threat Intelligence Platform
talks.teaser: Presents a self-hosted platform that organizes and searches threat reports by context rather than raw indicators.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem in cyber threat intelligence: teams must absorb and produce information quickly, yet many threat intelligence platforms concentrate on technical indicators rather than context. Reports end up spread across paid vendor portals, PDF folders on individual analysts' desktops, and blogs that can disappear. Knowledge is lost when subject matter experts leave, and searching across all of these sources is slow, especially when adversaries keep changing how they write up observables.

The speaker introduces DocIntel, a web application that acts as a central, searchable repository for threat reports. Users read documents in the browser, search with filters, and organize material with tags grouped into facets such as geography, software and source. Reports arrive by upload or automated collection, and the tool pre-processes them by extracting metadata, tags and observables using keywords and regular expressions. An analyst then reviews the result, corrects titles and classifications, and the system learns which extracted URLs to ignore over time. Access is controlled through groups, with multi-factor authentication, LDAP integration and audit logs of who viewed which document.

The tool is written in .NET, runs under Docker, and is open source, with commercial support offered on request. The speaker says it scales to hundreds of thousands of documents with some tuning, and mentions a planned Python API client and documentation still in progress. He also invited feed providers to help build connectors. In the Q&A, binary file storage was noted as not yet supported. The main takeaway is to keep threat knowledge centralized and contextual instead of relying on folders and indicator lists.

talks.title: News From The Automation Department
talks.teaser: Shows how exposure data about vulnerable Exchange servers gets turned into automated notices to their owners.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical gap: exposure data from leaked scan results gives only bare IP addresses for hosts with recently disclosed Exchange Server vulnerabilities. Looking up owners through WHOIS and DNS rarely produces a usable contact quickly, so the speaker's team built a pipeline to reach the responsible people faster.

The pipeline pulls results from the LeakIX API with a Go client, then resolves each IP to its DNS names and alternate domain names using OpenSSL. A validation step runs an Nmap script, written by a colleague for Exchange issues, to check whether a host is still exposed to the latest referenced attacks. WHOIS and DNS lookups then produce candidate email addresses, which can be corrected or extended by hand when the list looks thin. A notification template is attached, and a ticket is opened that sends the condensed advisory to the contacts. A live demo showed this flow end to end for one organisation whose server had been patched but was not fully covered by the check.

The second part concerns a large MISP community of roughly 3,000 users across about 1,500 organisations, many of them external and therefore outside the speaker's control. Bounce messages from departed users or full mailboxes were piling up, so a small script collects them from a mailbox fed by Postfix and Exchange bounce notices, extracts the addresses, runs sanity checks, and then either disables email notifications or disables the account. The takeaway is that modest glue scripts around existing APIs and mail handling can keep both outreach and user hygiene manageable at scale.
